Worked Solution

Class intervals Class boundaries(Ksh) Midpoint of intervals \((X_i)\) Frequencies \((f)\) Cumulative frequency \((cf)\) \(fX_i\) \(f(X_i-\mu)^2\)
\({@lower_range1@}-{@upper_range1@}\) \({@float(lower_bound1)@}-{@float(upper_bound1)@}\) \({@midpoints[1]@}\) \({@f1@}\) \({@cf[1]@}\) \({@fxi[1]@}\) \({@mean_fdiffs[1]@}\)
\({@lower_range2@}-{@upper_range2@}\) \({@float(lower_bound2)@}-{@float(upper_bound2)@}\) \({@midpoints[2]@}\) \({@f2@}\) \({@cf[2]@}\) \({@fxi[2]@}\) \({@mean_fdiffs[2]@}\)
\({@lower_range3@}-{@upper_range3@}\) \({@float(lower_bound3)@}-{@float(upper_bound3)@}\) \({@midpoints[3]@}\) \({@f3@}\) \({@cf[3]@}\) \({@fxi[3]@}\) \({@mean_fdiffs[3]@}\)
\({@lower_range4@}-{@upper_range4@}\) \({@float(lower_bound4)@}-{@float(upper_bound4)@}\) \({@midpoints[4]@}\) \({@f4@}\) \({@cf[4]@}\) \({@fxi[4]@}\) \({@mean_fdiffs[4]@}\)
\({@lower_range5@}-{@upper_range5@}\) \({@float(lower_bound5)@}-{@float(upper_bound5)@}\) \({@midpoints[5]@}\) \({@f5@}\) \({@cf[5]@}\) \({@fxi[5]@}\) \({@mean_fdiffs[5]@}\)
\(\sum f={@n@}\) \(\sum fX_i={@sum_fxi@}\) \(\sum{f(X_i-\mu)^2}={@mean_squared_diffs@}\)

Using the information in the table above, we will compute the following statistics:

(a) Mean \( \displaystyle \bar{x}=\frac{\sum{fX}}{\sum{f}}=\frac{{@sum_fxi@}}{{@n@}}={@mean@}\)

(b) Median

The median class is that class containing the \( \displaystyle \left( \frac{{@total_f@}}{2}\right)\) item \(={@median_cf@}^{\text{th}}\)item.

Therefore, the median class is \({@float(lower_bound)@}-{@float(upper_bound)@}\).

Thus \(B_L={@float(lower_bound)@}, \, \displaystyle \left( \frac{n}{2}\right)={@median_cf@}, \, f_c={@f_median@}, \, i={@float(upper_bound)@}-{@float(lower_bound)@}={@width@}, \, cf_b={@cf_lower@} \)

Therefore,

\( \begin{align} \displaystyle md &=B_L+ \left( \frac{\frac{N}{2}-cf_b}{f_c}\right) \cdot i \\ &={@float(lower_bound)@}+ \left( \frac{\frac{{@total_f@}}{2}-{@cf_lower@}}{{@f_median@}}\right) \cdot {@width@} \\ &={@float(lower_bound)@}+{@md1@} \\ &={@ta@} \end{align}\)

The median cost is \( \text{Ksh} \, {@ta@}\).

(c) Mode

When dealing with grouped data, the mode represents the value or values in a dataset that have the highest frequency.

To calculate the mode for our grouped data, we will use the following formula:

\(\displaystyle \text{Mode}=L+\left( \frac{f_1 - f_0}{(f_1 - f_0)+(f_1 - f_2)}\right )\cdot h\)

Where:

  • \( L={@float(Lm)@}\): Lower boundary of the modal class (class with the highest frequency)
  • \(f_1={@f1m@}\): Frequency of the modal class
  • \(f_0={@f0m@}\): Frequency of the class preceding the modal class
  • \(f_2={@f2m@}\): Frequency of the class succeeding the modal class
  • \(h={@hm@}\): Class width (the difference between upper and lower boundaries of each class)

      • \(\displaystyle \text{Mode}={@float(Lm)@}+\left( \frac{{@f1m@}- {@f0m@}}{({@f1m@}- {@f0m@})+({@f1m@} - {@f2m@})}\right )\cdot {@hm@}={@Mode@}\)

      This formula allows us to estimate the mode for grouped data by taking into account the relative frequencies of the modal class and its neighbouring classes.

      It's important to note that the mode for grouped data is an estimate and may not represent an exact value within the dataset.

      (d) Standard deviation \( \displaystyle \sigma = \sqrt{\frac{\sum{f(x-\bar{x})^2}}{\sum f}}= \sqrt{\frac{{@mean_squared_diffs@}}{{@n@}}}={@standard_deviation@}\)

      Finding \(Q_1\)

      \(Q_1\) is \(\left (\frac{{@total_frequencies@}}{4}\right )\) item i.e \({@q1@}^{th}\) item which falls in the \({@class_q1@}^{@power_Q1@}\)class, \(cf={@choosing_cf@},f={@choosing_freq@}\) and \(i={@class_size@}\)

      \(Q_1={@bd_q1@}+\left(\frac{\frac{{@total_frequencies@}}{4}-{@choosing_cf@}}{{@choosing_freq@}}\right )\times {@class_size@}\)

      \(Q_1={@bd_q1@}+{@soln2@}\)

      \(Q_1={@ta1@}\)

      Finding \(Q_2\)

      \(Q_2\) is \(\left (\frac{2}{4}\times{@total_frequencies@}\right )\) item i.e \({@q2@}^{th}\) item which falls in the \({@class_q2@}^{@power_Q2@}\)class, \(cf={@choosing_cf_q2@},f={@choosing_freq_q2@}\) and\(i={@class_size@}\)

      \(Q_2={@bd_q2@}+\left(\frac{\frac{{2}}{4}\times{@total_frequencies@}-{@choosing_cf_q2@}}{{@choosing_freq_q2@}}\right )\times {@class_size@}\)

      \(Q_2={@bd_q2@}+{@soln4@}\)

      \(Q_1={@ta2@}\)

      Finding \(Q_3\)

      \(Q_3\) is \(\left ( \frac{3}{4} \times{@total_frequencies@}\right )\) item i.e \({@q3@}^{th}\) item which falls in the \({@class_q3@}^{@power_Q3@}\)class, \(cf={@choosing_cf_q3@},f={@choosing_freq_q3@}\) and \(i={@class_size@}\)

      \(Q_3={@bd_q3@}+\left(\frac{\frac{{3}}{4}\times{@total_frequencies@}-{@choosing_cf_q3@}}{{@choosing_freq_q3@}}\right )\times {@class_size@}\)

      \(Q_3={@bd_q3@}+{@soln6@}\)

      \(Q_3={@ta3@}\)

      (h) Karl Pearson’s Coefficient of Skewness \((SK)=\displaystyle\frac{\text{mean}-\text{mode}}{\text{standard deviation}}\)

      \(\begin{align} (SK)&=\displaystyle\frac{\text{mean}-\text{mode}}{\text{standard deviation}}\\ &= \displaystyle\frac{{@mean@}-{@Mode@}}{{@standard_deviation@}}\\ &=\displaystyle {@skewness@}\\ \end{align} \)

      Bowleys Coefficient of Skewness (Sk) \(\displaystyle\frac{Q_3-Q_1-2 \cdot \text{median}}{Q_3-Q_1}\)

      \(\begin{align} \text{Bowleys Coefficient(SK)}&=\displaystyle\frac{Q_3-Q_1-2(\text{median})}{Q_3-Q_1}\\ &=\displaystyle\frac{{@ta3@}+{@ta1@}-2 ({@ta@})}{{@ta3@}-{@ta1@}}\\ &={@bowley_sk@}\\ \end{align} \)
